title: Client integration fastpath and canonical workarounds
author: Maya Chen
content:
Title: Client integration fastpath and canonical workarounds

Summary:
This page is a compact, production-ready playbook for product and platform engineers integrating Redwood's API/SDKs into customer-facing services. It focuses on a small set of starter templates, recommended runtime configuration, observability mappings, and the canonical fixes we repeatedly apply during support escalations. Use this as the 30–90 minute integration roadmap and the first-stop triage playbook for common runtime problems.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: backend engineers, platform engineers, SREs, and SDK maintainers.
- Scope: SDK initialization, request patterns (sync/streaming/batching), canary checklist, standard metrics/logs, and top 6 canonical fixes.

Quickstart: minimal server-side integration (Python)
1) Install SDK
   pip install redwood-sdk-client==1.4.0  # recommended stable release for 2026

2) Minimal example (thread-safe client, connection pooling):
```python
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY", max_connections=50, timeout_ms=7000)

response = client.generate(model="redwood-medium-v1", prompt="Summarize user message:\n\n" + user_message, max_tokens=150)
print(response.text)
```
Notes:
- Use environment variables for keys and rotate with your secret manager.
- max_connections controls local connection pool; tune to your worker concurrency.

Node/HTTP curl example (quick sanity):
```bash
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-small-v1","prompt":"Extract action items:\n- "}'
```

Starter adapter template (generic microservice pattern)
- Purpose: uniform wrapper to centralize retries, cost guards, and telemetry.
- Responsibilities:
  - Token budgeting (max_tokens per request)
  - Function-call routing for tools
  - Backoff & retry policy centralized
  - Metrics tags: model, route, customer_tier, prompt_template

Adapter config example (YAML):
| key | example | description |
|-----|---------|-------------|
| model | redwood-medium-v1 | Default model for route |
| max_prompt_tokens | 1024 | Trim user input beyond this threshold |
| retry_policy | exponential: base=200ms, max=5 | Retries on 429 & 5xx except 501/502 special-cases |
| stream_timeout_ms | 20000 | Per-request streaming idle timeout |

Observability mapping (minimal required metrics & logs)
Required metrics (emit as Prometheus or StatsD):
- redwood_request_count{route,model,result_code}  # success, client_error, server_error, rate_limited
- redwood_request_latency_ms{route,model,p95,p99}
- redwood_token_usage{route,model,token_type}  # prompt vs completion
- redwood_stream_disconnects_total{route,reason}

Structured log fields (append in JSON logs):
- request_id, session_id, model, model_version, route, tokens_prompt, tokens_completion, status_code, latency_ms, retry_count

Canary checklist (pre-rollout, applies to SDK upgrades, model swaps, or config changes)
1) Unit + integration tests: include snapshot tests for prompt templates.
2) Traffic split: route 98% stable, 2% canary for 30 minutes.
3) Alert hooks: create an ephemeral alert for p95 latency > 2x baseline or error rate > 0.5%.
4) Manual quality gate: run a small eval prompt set (20 inputs) measuring semantic similarity > 0.9 against baseline embeddings.
5) Observability smoke: verify token usage metric and trace context propagation.

Top support issues and canonical fixes (empirically most common)
1) Symptom: intermittent 429s during traffic bursts
   Canonical fixes:
   - Implement exponential backoff + jitter (base 200ms, max 6s, attempt cap 6).
   - Add local admission control: circuit-breaker that rejects low-priority background requests when inflight > X (X = concurrency * 4).
   - For user-visible requests, queue briefly (25–100 ms) to allow the serving runtime to batch efficiently.

   Example retry snippet (pseudocode):
   - if status == 429 or 5xx:
       sleep(backoff_with_jitter())
       retry up to N

2) Symptom: streaming responses terminate mid-token or client sees EOF
   Canonical fixes:
   - Ensure SDK/HTTP client supports keep-alives and per-chunk timeouts.
   - Increase stream_idle_timeout to 20s for mobile networks and 5s for LAN.
   - Server-side: verify you are using the streaming endpoint ("/v1/stream") and not an SDK wrapper that buffers.

   Diagnostic commands:
   - curl with --no-buffer and watch chunk boundaries; capture TCP level resets with ss/netstat.

3) Symptom: embedding vectors drift or mismatch across calls
   Canonical fixes:
   - Explicitly pin model version in production (model: text-embedding-2025-10).
   - Add a compatibility test in CI that compares embeddings for a fixed prompt set within cosine similarity thresholds.

4) Symptom: unexpectedly high token usage/cost
   Canonical fixes:
   - Enforce input pruning rules and token-aware truncation: keep last N tokens of conversation when summarizing.
   - Use streaming completion with max_tokens set conservatively.
   - Employ instruction templates that request concise output (e.g., "Respond in <= 40 words").

5) Symptom: auth failures after a secret rotation
   Canonical fixes:
   - Validate clock drift (some internal short-lived tokens require < 30s drift).
   - Add a readiness probe post-rotation that attempts a lightweight /v1/health call and falls back to cached credentials for 30s.

6) Symptom: high p99 latency when batching-enabled
   Canonical fixes:
   - Check batching window config: lower it for latency-sensitive routes (20ms) or increase for throughput routes (100–250ms).
   - Add priority routing: small requests routed to low-batch fast-path, large batched payloads to throughput path.

Triage runbook (first 10 minutes)
1) Reproduce: run the failing request locally against the same model version using the exact prompt.
2) Gather: request_id, model, route, timestamps, client logs, SDK version, and last config change.
3) Check metrics: increase in redwood_request_count and redwood_request_latency_ms; check for correlated infra alerts.
4) Quick mitigations: reduce traffic to the affected route, increase capacity if Dedicated, or enable automatic fallback to a cheaper model for non-critical requests.
5) Escalate: if error rate > 5% for 10m or p99 latency > 3s for user-critical routes, page oncall SRE and attach trace and a reproducible curl snippet.

Template: reproducible curl snippet to include in tickets
```bash
curl -v -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-medium-v1","prompt":"<paste prompt here>","max_tokens":150,"stream":false}'
```

Testing and CI recommendations
- Add a lightweight integration stage that runs once per PR with a small set of canary prompts (10–20). Fail if embedding drift or generation regression exceeds thresholds.
- Run nightly stability tests under synthetic burst traffic to surface 429 patterns.

Rollout notes for SDK upgrades
- Follow semantic versioning; prefer non-breaking patches for security fixes.
- When rolling an SDK with changed defaults (timeouts, retries), use the canary checklist above and include a migration doc in the release notes.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience. For escalations: oncall-eng-sre@redwood.ai.
- SDK maintainers: Maya Chen, Arjun Patel.

Appendix A — Useful command snippets
- Check health endpoint:
  curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health | jq
- Trace sampling quick check (look for trace_id in response headers):
  curl -I https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY"

Appendix B — Sample evaluation prompts for canary quality gate
1) Summarization: "Summarize the following thread into 3 bullets"
2) Extraction: "List all named entities and roles"
3) Instruction following: "Convert this prose into a terse checklist"
